message-authentication-code: A short tag computed from a message and a secret key, which only key holders can produce or check. It detects deliberate tampering, unlike a plain hash, which anyone can recompute. HMAC is a common construction. → A keyed authentication tag computed from a message and a shared secret. A secure scheme lets key holders check integrity and key possession; others can guess tags, with a probability depending on tag length and the scheme. It does not distinguish between holders of the same key.; source https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Message_authentication_code → https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104

key-pair: A matching public key and private key generated together. In passkeys the device keeps the private key and the server stores only the public key. → Related public and private keys used by a public-key scheme. A WebAuthn relying party stores the credential public key; private-key material remains with the authenticator or an authorised credential synchronisation or backup mechanism.; source https://www.w3.org/TR/webauthn-2/ → https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html

uniformly-random: Chosen so that every possible value is exactly as likely as every other. Entropy formulas assume this; human choices are far from uniform. → Chosen so that every possible value is equally likely. The simple logarithm-of-possibilities entropy formula assumes uniform selection; general entropy measures also describe non-uniform distributions.

rate-limiting: Capping how many requests or attempts a client, account or address may make in a period of time. It slows guessing and floods without locking accounts outright. → Capping how many requests or attempts a client, account or address may make in a period. It can slow guessing or floods, but its policy can also delay legitimate users or create denial-of-service risks.

sql-injection: A vulnerability where user input is pasted into a database query so that it is run as SQL code, letting an attacker read, change or delete data. Parameterised queries prevent it. → A vulnerability where untrusted input changes the structure or meaning of a SQL query. Parameterised queries keep bound values separate from SQL syntax; dynamic identifiers or SQL fragments still require safe construction and allowlists.; source https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/SQL_Injection → https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html

parameterised-query: A database query where user values are passed separately from the SQL text, so they are always treated as data, never as code. It prevents SQL injection. → A query that binds supplied values separately from SQL syntax, preventing those values from becoming SQL instructions. Identifiers such as table names generally cannot be bound as values; construct any dynamic SQL safely.

data-access-layer: The single module through which application code reads and writes the database. Making it require a tenant context enforces tenant filters in one place. → An application layer through which code reads and writes stored data. Requiring trustworthy tenant context can centralise isolation checks, provided all relevant paths use the layer; review or lint alone cannot prove complete enforcement.

bell-lapadula: A 1970s mandatory access control model for confidentiality: subjects may not read above their level (no read up) or write below it (no write down), so secrets cannot flow downwards. → A confidentiality model developed by David Bell and Leonard LaPadula in the 1970s. Its simplified level-only rules deny reading above the operating level and writing below it; real policies include labels, discretionary restrictions and trusted exceptions, so the slogan alone is not a deployment proof.

star-property: The Bell–LaPadula rule that a subject may not write to an object at a lower level, so a Trojan horse running at Secret cannot copy Secret data into an Unclassified file. → A Bell–LaPadula information-flow restriction commonly summarised as no write down. In the simplified level-only model without trusted exceptions, a Secret process cannot write Secret information to an Unclassified object.

windows-mic: Windows' integrity labelling system: processes and objects have levels such as low, medium and high, and by default a lower-level process cannot write to a higher-level object. Browser sandboxes run at low integrity. → Windows Mandatory Integrity Control labels subjects and objects with integrity levels. Its default policy blocks lower-integrity writes to higher-integrity objects; additional label policies and other permissions matter. Some browser sandbox designs use low or untrusted integrity levels.

secrets-manager: A service that stores passwords, API keys and other secrets encrypted, controls who can read them and logs every access, instead of leaving them in files or scripts. → A service that manages sensitive values such as passwords or API keys with access controls and protected storage. Rotation and audit coverage depend on the service, configuration and paths used; placing a secret there does not guarantee every use is logged.

shadow-it: Systems and services staff use without the IT department's approval, often to get around controls that are too painful. They escape security monitoring and policy. → Systems or services used without the organisation's usual IT approval or management. They can bypass intended security controls or inventory; their actual visibility and risk depend on the deployment.

ioc: A concrete artefact that suggests an intrusion, such as a malicious file hash, IP address or domain name. Precise but easy for attackers to change. → An observable artefact suggesting possible compromise, such as a file hash, address or domain. Its reliability and the attacker's cost of changing it depend on the indicator and context.

artefacts: Traces an attack leaves on machines or in traffic, such as registry keys, file names, unusual URL patterns or protocol quirks. Changing them takes the attacker more effort than changing an IP address. → Observable traces on hosts or networks, such as registry keys, file names, URL patterns or protocol features. The Pyramid of Pain places them above addresses as an adaptation-cost heuristic, not a guarantee that every artefact is harder to change.

network-segmentation: Dividing a network into zones with controlled traffic between them, so a compromised workstation cannot reach servers' admin interfaces. → Dividing a network into zones and controlling traffic between them. Properly enforced rules can restrict movement to sensitive interfaces; a zone boundary alone does not guarantee isolation.

hardened-workstation: A locked-down computer used only for administration, without email or web browsing, so admin credentials are not exposed to phishing or malware on everyday machines. → A workstation configured and managed for sensitive tasks, such as privileged administration, with reduced exposure to ordinary browsing and email. It reduces credential exposure but cannot guarantee that phishing or malware is impossible.

ci-cd: Continuous integration and continuous delivery or deployment: the automated pipeline that builds, tests and ships code. It holds production credentials, so compromising it can change what runs in production. → Continuous integration and continuous delivery or deployment: practices and automation for building, testing and delivering changes. A pipeline may hold credentials or influence production artifacts, so its compromise can threaten releases; independent controls can restrict that influence.

encryption-in-transit: Encrypting data while it moves across a network, usually with TLS, so eavesdroppers cannot read or silently alter it. → Encryption of data while it moves between systems. Properly validated authenticated protocols such as TLS protect confidentiality and integrity between their endpoints; encryption alone does not establish integrity or protect data beyond those endpoints.

presigned-url: A URL containing a signature that grants whoever has it a specific action on one object, such as GET on one S3 file, until it expires. → A URL containing a signature that permits a specified operation on a resource subject to its validity conditions. S3 presigned URLs are bearer-like but can stop working before their stated expiry if signing credentials expire or are revoked, or applicable policy denies the request.

oauth: A standard framework that lets an application obtain limited, delegated access to an API on a user's behalf, using access tokens instead of the user's password. → An authorisation framework for obtaining limited access to protected resources using access tokens. It includes delegated user-authorised flows and client-credentials flows where a client acts on its own behalf; OAuth alone is not a login-identity protocol.

sparse: Mostly empty. In an access control matrix most subjects have no rights on most objects, so storing the full table wastes space. → A matrix with mostly zero or empty entries. In an access-control matrix, many subject–object pairs often have no rights, making a dense representation wasteful.

real-uid: On Unix, the ID of the user who actually started a process. A setuid program keeps the caller's real user ID while running with a different effective one. → A Unix process identity normally inherited from its parent and retained across ordinary setuid-program execution. It commonly identifies the caller, but privileged programs can change it, so it is not an immutable record of who started a process.

symlink: A file that points to another path. Opening it opens the target instead, which attackers exploit in TOCTOU races. → A file containing a pathname used to resolve another object. Many operations follow it, while others can inspect the link itself or reject following it; changing a link between pathname checks can create a race.; source https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbolic_link → https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/symlink.7.html

etc-passwd: The Unix file listing user accounts, writable only by root. Writing attacker data to it can create or change accounts. → A Unix-like account database file containing account names, IDs and other fields, normally publicly readable but restricted for writing. Password hashes are normally stored separately on shadow-password systems; unauthorised writes can alter account definitions.; source https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passwd#Password_file → https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/passwd.5.html

cache-control: The HTTP header that tells browsers and shared caches whether and how long they may store a response. private forbids shared caches from storing it; no-store forbids storing it anywhere. → An HTTP header controlling cache behaviour. An unqualified private directive forbids conforming shared caches from storing the response; no-store directs caches not to store it, but cannot guarantee deletion of copies already stored or stop malicious recipients.

domain-controller: A Windows server that runs Active Directory: it holds the accounts and passwords for a Windows domain and authenticates logins across it. Compromising it gives control of the domain. → A server providing directory and authentication services for an Active Directory domain. Writable controllers hold sensitive account and credential data; compromise can endanger domain control. Read-only domain controllers have different storage and replication restrictions.; source https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_controller_(Windows) → https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/plan/security-best-practices/appendix-b--privileged-accounts-and-groups-in-active-directory

vpn: Virtual private network: an encrypted tunnel that connects a remote device or site to a private network as if it were directly attached. A VPN concentrator or appliance is the gateway that terminates many such tunnels. → A restricted logical network built over shared infrastructure, often using encrypted tunnels for remote or site-to-site access. Encryption and routing guarantees depend on the VPN design; the gateway or concentrator terminates connections.; source https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_private_network → https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4949

access-point: The device that radio clients connect to on a Wi-Fi network and that bridges them onto the wired network. In enterprise Wi-Fi it hands the authentication decision to a RADIUS server. → A Wi-Fi device through which wireless clients access a network, commonly bridging them to other network links. Enterprise deployments often use an external authentication service such as RADIUS; architecture and configuration vary.

http-5xx: The family of HTTP status codes (500 to 599) meaning the server failed to handle a valid request. 503 Service Unavailable means the server is temporarily unable to serve it, for example when overloaded. → The HTTP server-error status family: the server knows it has erred or cannot perform the request. 503 Service Unavailable means temporary inability, commonly from overload or maintenance; a server failure does not prove the request was otherwise valid.

accounting-aaa: The AAA function that records who did what, when and from where. It supports detecting attacks, investigating incidents, evidence for disputes and, originally, billing for network access. → The AAA function that collects usage and event records associated with identities and sessions. It supports billing for network access, monitoring, investigation and evidence; completeness and attribution depend on trustworthy collection.

oidc: OpenID Connect: a login protocol built on OAuth 2.0 in which an identity provider tells an application who the user is, using a signed ID token. → OpenID Connect: an identity layer built on OAuth 2.0. It uses an ID token containing authentication claims that the client must validate; tokens are normally signed, with narrowly specified exceptions in the code flow.

saml: Security Assertion Markup Language: an XML-based standard for single sign-on, in which an identity provider sends a signed assertion about the user to an application. Common in enterprise SSO. → Security Assertion Markup Language: an XML-based framework for exchanging assertions about identity and attributes, widely used for enterprise single sign-on. The chosen profile and binding determine required signature, encryption and transport checks.; source https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Security_Assertion_Markup_Language → https://docs.oasis-open.org/security/saml/v2.0/saml-core-2.0-os.pdf
secf-accounting-evidence.md: **Billing**, which is where the term came from in network access. → **Billing** for metered network access.

cache-key: The information a cache uses to decide whether two requests can share a stored response, often the URL. If it ignores who is asking, one user can receive another's data. → Information used to choose a stored response for a request, often including the target URL and other selecting fields. Personalised responses need a safe caching policy covering relevant authenticated user and permission context; a tenant identifier alone may be insufficient.

security-key: A small hardware device, usually USB or NFC, that stores private keys and signs login challenges (FIDO2/WebAuthn). It is phishing-resistant. → A hardware authenticator, commonly connected by USB or NFC, that can hold credential private keys and sign RP-bound authentication data through FIDO2/WebAuthn. Phishing resistance depends on conforming client behaviour and correct relying-party validation.

web-origin: The scheme, host and port a web page came from, such as https://bank.com. Browsers report it to WebAuthn, so a phishing page on a different origin cannot use the bank's credential. → For ordinary web URLs, an origin is the scheme, host and port. WebAuthn client data includes the calling origin; browser RP-scope checks and the relying party's expected-origin validation together prevent an unrelated phishing site from using the credential for login.
shadow-it: source https://www.cs.virginia.edu/~evans/cs551/saltzer/ → https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-cloud-apps/tutorial-shadow-it

message-authentication-code: A keyed authentication tag computed from a message and a shared secret. A secure scheme lets key holders check integrity and key possession; others can guess tags, with a probability depending on tag length and the scheme. It does not distinguish between holders of the same key. → A keyed tag providing integrity and data-origin authentication under a shared secret. A secure scheme makes new-tag forgery difficult, rather than impossible; success probability depends on the scheme and tag length. A MAC gives neither confidentiality nor freshness, and cannot distinguish holders of the same key.; aliases ['MACs', 'message authentication codes'] → ['MACs', 'message authentication codes', 'MAC']

authorCorrections: Count entropy over a specified probability model; human choices also have entropy, but alphabet-times-length formulas do not model their distribution.
NIST password managers/autofill SHALL and paste SHOULD are distinct. OpenSSL default memory is version-specific rather than universal.
Hash collisions are possible; public/private schemes do not universally undo each other; signatures attribute to keys under binding assumptions.
WebAuthn signs authenticator data plus client-data hash, and RP/origin checks are required; synchronised passkeys are not permanently device-bound.
Offline backups and immutable backups are distinct. Split opposite aliases for unsalted versus salted and fast hashes versus password hashing.
Bare MAC resolves to a cryptographic term from a later security module; active mandatory-access-control contexts now use the full unambiguous phrase.
Remove broad misleading aliases such as FORCE, domain credentials, domain-joined, long-lived keys under short-lived credentials and generic digital signature aliases.
Qualify CloudTrail event coverage, KMS auditing/storage, root and setuid powers, Windows macro rollout, local admin propagation and behavioural-detection guarantees.
Explicitly teach PostgreSQL RLS bypass roles/whole-table limits, tenant-context trust and connection-pool reset before the corresponding question.
Simplified unsalted multi-target timing also assumes digest lookup does not bottleneck; attack-tree and ordinal risk arithmetic retain explicit assumptions.

analogyReview.scope: All 27 active lessons: 21 added analogy callouts reviewed for mapping, limit, placement and visible prerequisites; 6 lessons recorded as not needing one.

secf-security-properties.rationale: Posted-contract analogy maps reading, page swapping and late delivery to C, I and A; the seal limit correctly points to the trusted-reference problem and the copy-without-loss limit to silent confidentiality breaches.

secf-security-tradeoffs.rationale: Single-house-key analogy maps encryption key loss to availability loss and spare keys to backups; the limit (no locksmith for a strong lost key; data copied without loss) is accurate.

secf-identity-permission.rationale: Hotel check-in maps name, passport, room-specific key card and lock log to the four AAA steps; the bearer-card limit correctly mirrors stolen session tokens.

secf-accounting-evidence.rationale: Shop CCTV recorder maps back-office storage to logs on production hosts and off-site recording to a separately administered collector; limits (source can omit or forge events; account is not a person) match the lesson.

secf-system-boundaries.rationale: Airport landside/airside screening maps to a trust boundary, with staff and cargo routes as forgotten flows such as queues and partner feeds; limit (threats inside; a drawn boundary checks nothing by itself) is accurate.

secf-stride-threats.rationale: STRIDE is itself a mnemonic checklist with concrete everyday examples in its table; an extra comparison would repeat the system-boundaries analogy.

secf-attack-tree-costs.rationale: Burglar choosing window or front door maps OR to choosing the easier route and AND to adding lock-picking and alarm costs; limit (no exact costs, incomplete knowledge) is honest.

secf-risk-responses.rationale: House maintenance maps roof repair, tree removal, insurance and a tolerated scuff to mitigate, eliminate, transfer and accept; limit (organisational authority, insurance exclusions, reputational harm) is accurate.

secf-least-privilege-design.rationale: Valet key that starts the car but not the boot/glovebox (some cars; Wikipedia car-key article) maps to a narrowly scoped credential; verifier softened "limits are fixed" to "usually fixed". Limit (permissions drift; holder can still drive away) is accurate.

secf-layers-defaults.rationale: Party guest list versus banned list maps to allowlist versus denylist defaults; limit (doorkeeper judgement; unreadable list = fail-open/closed choice) is accurate.

secf-mediation-open-design.rationale: Unmarked stage door maps a front-of-house check to UI hiding and the back door to an unchecked API, linking complete mediation and open design; limit (cached decisions and TOCTOU have no simple physical equivalent) is accurate.

secf-shared-authority-usability.rationale: Two-key safe deposit box maps to two independent conditions (separation of privilege, MFA, separation of duties); limit (both keys through one compromised account or a bypass) is accurate.

secf-factors-password-failures.rationale: Bank card plus PIN maps possession and knowledge factors; the skimmer limit is supported (skimmers can capture card data including the PIN) and correctly parallels real-time phishing of password plus OTP.

secf-random-password-entropy.rationale: Combination bike lock maps dials to random symbols and ten digits to choices per symbol (about 3.3 bits per dial, recomputed); limit (owner-chosen codes; attacking the lock itself) is accurate.

secf-password-policy.rationale: A list of normative policy rules; the factor and lockout ideas already have analogies in neighbouring lessons, and another comparison would not clarify SHALL/SHOULD.

secf-password-storage.rationale: The salt/slow-hash comparison lives in the next lesson's locker analogy; repeating it here would add no understanding.

secf-guessing-costs.rationale: Wall of combination lockers maps one code tried on every locker to unsalted hashes, per-locker tries to salts and a minute per try to a slow hash; limit (more hardware; common codes still fall early) is accurate.

secf-phishing-resistant-login.rationale: Code read aloud versus a key cut for one door maps TOTP relay versus origin-bound WebAuthn; limit (private key never leaves the authenticator; sessions and recovery bypass login) is accurate.

secf-permission-matrix.rationale: Guest list versus ticket maps ACL-with-object versus capability-with-subject, including delegation; limit (unforgeability; revocation needs expiry rules) is accurate.

secf-unix-dac.rationale: Octal notation and the first-match rule are concrete procedures shown directly with ls output; an analogy would not add understanding.

secf-mandatory-labels.rationale: Classification levels are already the real-world setting and the directional table is concrete; another analogy would repeat it.

secf-policy-models.rationale: Hospital badges map role, shift/ward attributes and patient assignment to RBAC, ABAC and ReBAC; limit (software has no judgement; attributes must come from trusted records) is accurate.

secf-object-authorisation.rationale: Theatre cloakroom maps audience membership to authentication and coat-ownership checking to object-level authorisation; limit (unguessable peg numbers do not fix a missing check) is accurate.

secf-kill-chain-stages.rationale: Staged burglary maps the seven Lockheed Martin stages in order; limit (key holders/insiders skip stages; loops; unseen preparation) matches the lesson's criticisms.

secf-attack-vocabulary.rationale: The why/how distinction is shown directly with concrete technique IDs and a report sentence; an analogy would add little.

secf-intrusion-defence.rationale: Burglar using the owner's ladder maps legitimate tools (PowerShell, WMI, cloud CLIs) and hash-matching versus behavioural detection; limit (telemetry and tested rules needed; admins also act unusually) is accurate.

secf-detection-evidence.rationale: Shoplifter red coat versus method maps indicators versus TTPs on the Pyramid of Pain; limit (behavioural false alarms; telemetry coverage) is accurate.
